summary: Recommends that authors writing IANA Considerations sections consider assigning a small range of numbers for experimentation and testing. People experimenting with protocols often need a protocol number or constant, even in closed environments. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: If you invent a new game, you need a place to try rules without taking over someone's real game. This says to set aside a few spare numbers for testing so experiments do not clash.

subtitle: Reserve a few protocol numbers for testing instead of lending out temporary real ones.

tldr.problem: Experimenting with a protocol extension usually needs a protocol number or constant, but getting an official one can be hard, and temporary assignments are difficult to take back.
tldr.mechanism: Protocol authors should consider reserving a small range of numbers for experimentation in their IANA Considerations sections. Products must keep those numbers disabled by default, and IANA assigns IP protocol values 253 and 254 for this purpose.
tldr.outcome: Experimenters get numbers they can use without a formal assignment, with the understanding that such numbers are not unique and not for general deployment.

today: RFC 3692 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 82) that updates RFC 2434, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Experiments Need Numbers
sections.content:
Experimenting with or extending a protocol often needs a number as part of the implementation. A protocol that runs directly over IP needs an IP Protocol number in the Protocol field of the IP header, and a new DHCP option needs an option number. Sometimes this is easy, such as a TCP or UDP port for testing. Other times the name space is small, or the rules require strong community support, such as an "IETF Standards Action" in a Standards Track RFC.

The memo considers letting IANA make temporary assignments and rejects it for three reasons. Numbers are hard to reclaim because contact information goes out of date. If the number ends up in a product, it is hard to know whether reuse would harm deployed devices. And it can be hard to tell when an experiment has ended.
sections.eli5: Lending out a real number for a while is risky, because nobody remembers to give it back and someone may already be using it.

sections.title: A Reserved Experimental Range
sections.content:
The approach this RFC recommends is to assign a range of numbers specifically earmarked for testing and experimentation. Devices that agree to cooperate can use them for whatever they like, with the understanding that other implementations may use the same numbers for different experiments. They are similar to "Private Use" values in RFC 2434.

Most devices ignore such numbers. A router forwarding an IP datagram does not need to look at the Protocol field at all. A device that is sent an unknown extension will ignore the PDU, discard it or signal an error, depending on the protocol's rules, and only devices configured for the experiment process it further. Once an extension has proved useful, a permanent number can be obtained through the normal assignment procedures.
sections.eli5: It is like marking a few lockers at school as "for science fair only". Anyone can use them, but nobody can say a locker is theirs forever.

sections.title: Rules for Protocols and Products
sections.content:
Protocol documents should consider reserving a small set of numbers for experimentation, through an explicit reservation in an IANA Considerations section. The right amount depends on the protocol. If a field is split into ranges handled differently, such as "silently ignore" versus "return an error", one or more values from each sub-range may need to be reserved. Protocols that return error codes may also reserve a few experimental error values. In many cases, one value is enough, and reserving many may tempt people to treat one value as theirs alone.

Experimental numbers are never to be made permanent. When a product uses them, the shipping version must disable recognition by default, and in most cases must make the end user configure the value explicitly before enabling it. If the product has no user interface, it must require explicit re-programming, such as a firmware download or a feature card. The memo also says it would be inappropriate for vendors, a consortium or another standards body to agree on a value among themselves and deploy devices with it.
sections.eli5: The test lockers must start out switched off, and the person using them picks which locker. Companies cannot secretly agree that locker 7 is theirs.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and Existing Name Spaces
sections.content:
New values in the IP Protocol field normally need an IETF Standards Action per RFC 2780. For experimentation and testing, IANA has assigned two values, 253 and 254. They come from the upper end of the number space so that they stand out from existing assignments.

Many other name spaces have no values reserved for experimentation. Experimental values there can be assigned by publishing an RFC that documents the allocation, or, when that seems like overkill, through IESG Approval as described in RFC 2434.
sections.eli5: For the internet's protocol numbers, two spare numbers, 253 and 254, are now set aside for tryouts. For other lists, a group can still ask for tryout spots in the usual way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it has no known security implications. The text does warn, in its design discussion, that shipping a product with an experimental value pre-enabled can cause interoperability problems when the value collides with a different use. That is why the memo requires such features to be off by default.
sections.eli5: The memo does not see any safety problem, but it does say to keep the tryout features switched off until someone chooses to use them.
